items.text:
Compare results, monitor long-running tasks, or work across related conversations without repeatedly switching between sessions. Like in the editor window, the two-dimensional session grid in the Agents window lets you drag sessions into horizontal or vertical splits and resize the panes.

Maximize a session when you need to focus, then return to the grid to continue working across conversations.

items.title: Compact layout density
items.text:
Setting: window.density.layout

Fit more content in the Agents window with the Compact layout density. Compact density uses a shorter title bar, removes the gaps between workbench parts, and reduces pane spacing.

By default, the Agents window follows the user-level window.density.layout setting, which also applies to editor windows. To set a different density for the Agents window only, open it and choose View > Layout Density. The density of editor windows remains unchanged.

items.title: Additional session-filtering options
items.text:
Focus your sessions list on the work you care about. Open Filter Sessions to filter independently by:
- Environment: Where the session runs, such as locally, in the cloud, or on a remote host.
- Harness: Which agent harness the session uses.
- Created In: Which application created the session, such as VS Code, Copilot CLI, or the Copilot app.

The menu also brings together ordering, grouping, Show Done, and Created Externally controls.

items.title: Track activity across nested sessions
items.text:
Nested sessions let you split related work across separate conversations. In the Agents window, each nested session shows its unread status and last-modified time, helping you find recent activity and conversations that need your attention without opening them individually.

Status is tracked independently for each conversation:
- Opening a nested session marks only that conversation as read. An unread nested session does not make the main session appear unread.
- The last-modified time reflects activity in that conversation, not activity in the main session or another nested session.

Read status and last-modified times persist when you reload the window or restart VS Code.

To clear unread status for an entire session tree, right-click the main session and select Mark as Read. Unrelated sessions are not affected.

items.title: Simplified new-session controls (Experimental)
items.text:
Settings: sessions.chat.experimental.newSessionComposerLayout, sessions.chat.unifiedWorkspacePicker.enabled (Agents window only)

The experimental new-session composer keeps your prompt at the center while making session choices easier to review. Workspace, repository, and harness controls now appear in a collapsible Session Options tray above the chat input.

Getting-started tips now appear in a rounded notice below the chat input, so they no longer separate the session controls from your prompt.

Collapse the tray to reduce visual clutter without changing your selections. The composer remembers your choice, adapts labels as the window narrows, and keeps the options expanded when screen reader optimized mode is active. When you use a custom chat background, the tray has an opaque surface to keep its controls readable.

items.title: Improved context picker positioning
items.text: The Add Context picker now opens next to the button that invoked it and closes when you select the button again. This keeps the picker visually connected to the chat input in the editor and Agents windows.

items.title: Move agent picker in context control (Experimental)
items.text:
Setting: sessions.chat.experimental.agentsPickerInAttachContextMenu (Agents window only)

If you prefer to have the Agent picker initially hidden from the chat input to reduce the number of controls, you can configure this setting to move it into the Add Context menu. After you select an agent, the picker returns to the chat input.

items.title: Customize new-session welcome messages (Experimental)
items.text:
Settings: sessions.chat.experimental.welcomePhrases, sessions.chat.experimental.welcomeMessages (Agents window only)

New-session welcome messages add personality to the Agents window. In this release, you can add your own phrases to the defaults or replace the default phrases. Use the {name} placeholder to position your welcome name anywhere in a phrase.

Select Customize Welcome Message beside the heading to change your name or open the phrase setting. You can also right-click the heading and select Hide Welcome Message to turn welcome phrases off.

items.title: Continue local external Copilot sessions without reloading
items.text:
New conversations from the Copilot CLI and GitHub Copilot app are now picked up automatically as external sessions as soon as you send the first request, even when the Agents window is already open. You can open and continue these conversations directly from the Agents window.

Use the Created In and Created Externally filters to choose which conversations appear in the sessions list.

items.title: Codex chat handoff between apps
items.text:
Pick up a Codex chat started in the ChatGPT app or Codex CLI and continue it in VS Code's Agents window on the same machine, with your conversation history intact. You can switch back to the ChatGPT app or Codex CLI later and continue the same chat.

To use your GitHub Copilot subscription in VS Code, choose a Copilot model in the model picker. For example, you can keep working with Copilot after reaching your ChatGPT usage limit.

With Codex enabled and Created Externally sessions visible, chats created or updated in ChatGPT or Codex CLI appear within a few seconds without reloading VS Code.

Only one application can send messages to the chat at a time. If ChatGPT or Codex CLI still has the chat open, a This chat is open in another app banner in VS Code explains why sending is unavailable. Fully quit ChatGPT or exit the Codex CLI session, then select Retry. Your draft and attachments stay in place, and Retry checks access without sending your message.

items.title: Download remote files from the editor
items.text: Save an open remote file locally, without having to navigate for it in the Files panel. In the Agents window, open the editor's More Actions menu and select Download... to download the file to a local destination.

items.title: Dev Container samples (Experimental)
items.text:
Setting: chat.agentHost.devContainer.samples.enabled (Agents window only)

Try an agent with a ready-to-use development environment without first cloning a repository or installing its language tools locally. The Agents window now offers Dev Container samples for Go, .NET, Node.js, PHP, Python, and Rust.

Install and start Docker, and then enable the setting. Open a new session in the desktop Agents window, select Dev Container Sample from the workspace picker, and send a prompt.

This also requires chat.agentHost.devContainer.enabled and chat.remoteAgentHostsEnabled to be enabled.

items.title: Sandboxing in the Copilot agent host
items.text:
Settings: chat.agent.sandbox.enabled

Sandboxing gives you more control over what Copilot can access while working on a task. It limits how supported agent operations access files and network resources, and helps to reduce the impact of model mistakes, prompt injection, untrusted dependencies, and locally launched tool servers.

Depending on the operation and platform, these restrictions use operating-system protections or checks within the agent host process. Sandboxing adds a layer of protection, but does not replace endpoint security or provide a standalone security boundary.

Sandboxing is available on Windows, macOS, and Linux. On Windows, required operating-system updates must be installed. Refer to Check platform availability for more details.

To configure sandboxing for all your sessions, enable the chat.agent.sandbox.enabled setting. You can also control sandboxing at the session level with the Sandboxing for terminal toggle in the Permissions menu.

items.title: Persistent progress in chat
items.text:
Settings: chat.experimental.persistentProgress, chat.experimental.persistentProgressVerbosity

Persistent progress is rolling out to all users. It keeps in-progress responses visible and lets you control how much progress detail appears. Use chat.experimental.persistentProgress to choose among three icon variants, including a monochrome icon or no icon.

items.title: Meet Blobby
items.text:
The /vscode-pet has a name: Blobby. Type /vscode-pet in any chat in the editor or Agents window to meet Blobby.

Type /blobby to customize Blobby. More customization options become available as you explore chat and unlock achievements.

Learn more about Blobby and chat pets.

items.title: See discovered MCP servers in Customizations editor (Preview)
items.text:
Find MCP servers supplied by plugins, extensions, and built-in integrations alongside your configured servers in the MCP Servers section of the Agent Customizations editor. Servers discovered outside your workspace's mcp.json are visible in the UI, so you don't have to use MCP: List Servers to find them.

Run Chat: Open Customizations from the Command Palette and select MCP Servers to inspect the available integrations. Learn more about adding and managing MCP servers.

items.title: Frosted glass overlays and menus
items.text:
Settings: workbench.modernUIFrostedGlass, workbench.modernUIFrostedGlassOpacity

Menus, the Command Palette, and other pop-ups now use softly blurred, frosted glass backgrounds in the desktop Agents window. Frosted glass is also available in editor windows when the modernized UI is enabled with workbench.experimental.modernUI.

Use workbench.modernUIFrostedGlassOpacity to control how much of the blurred content shows through. Lower values make the background more transparent, while higher values make it more solid.

Frosted glass respects reduced-transparency preferences in VS Code and your operating system, and uses solid backgrounds with high contrast themes or when the effect isn't supported. Disable workbench.modernUIFrostedGlass if you notice display or performance issues.

items.title: Choose your tab style (Experimental)
items.text:
Setting: workbench.experimental.modernUIEditorTabStyle

When the modernized UI is enabled (workbench.experimental.modernUI), you can choose between two tab styles:
- connected: visually connect the active tab to its content.
- pill: display tabs as separate rounded pills.

items.title: Spreading block pasting
items.text:
Setting: editor.multiCursorPaste

Paste a copied block at a single cursor to distribute its rows across successive destination lines. This behavior is enabled by default when editor.multiCursorPaste is set to spread. Set it to full to paste the complete block instead.

items.title: Sign in to multiple GitHub Enterprise instances
items.text:
Setting: github-enterprise.uris

Many organizations use GitHub Copilot through a GHE.com account but keep their code on GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES). The github-enterprise.uri setting held a single instance, so you couldn't be signed in to both at once. For example, you couldn't use Copilot with your GHE.com account and review pull requests on GHES in the same VS Code window.

The new github-enterprise.uris setting takes a list of GHE.com and GHES instances:

``json
"github-enterprise.uris": [
"https://octocat.ghe.com",
"https://github.contoso.com"
]
`

The GitHub Enterprise authentication provider holds accounts from every instance in the list. Each account is labeled with its host, such as monalisa - octocat.ghe.com, so you can tell them apart in the Accounts menu. When more than one instance is configured, signing in asks which instance to use. The order of the entries doesn't select a default instance.

items.title: Migration of legacy VS Code policies to Agent Host managed settings
items.text:
The Copilot harness, powered by the Copilot SDK and running in VS Code's Agent Host, is gradually becoming the default for enterprise users who have VS Code experiments enabled. To preserve existing enterprise controls during this transition, VS Code translates supported legacy policies into unified managed settings at runtime when possible. This translation applies to sessions on the same machine and does not change your policy configuration.

Enterprises should still migrate to unified managed settings where applicable for consistent policy management across VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, and Copilot CLI.

items.title: Use managed settings to require sandboxing (Preview)
Attribute Agent Host sessions to users and machines
Keep your selected agent through policy checks
items.text: When your enterprise requires a fresh policy check with forceRemoteSettingsRefresh, chat preserves your selected agent during policy checks instead of switching to Ask or Edit. Routine background refreshes also keep the last accepted policy active while loading. Startup, account changes, and failed refreshes continue to block submissions until policy checks succeed. Newly accepted restrictions continue to apply.

items.title: GitHub Enterprise URI setting
items.text: The github-enterprise.uri setting is deprecated in favor of github-enterprise.uris, which accepts multiple GHE.com and GitHub Enterprise Server instances. VS Code still reads github-enterprise.uri when github-enterprise.uris isn't configured.

items.title: Legacy VS Code sandbox settings and device policies
items.text: Legacy VS Code sandbox settings and device policies are deprecated. ChatAgentSandboxEnabled now supplies an overridable default rather than a mandatory requirement in Agent Host. Local behavior is unchanged.

items.title: Release highlights
items.text:
This release adds shared canvases for agent workflows, lets you move chats without losing context, expands the Markdown editor, and gives administrators more control over agent permissions.
- Canvases (Preview): Collaborate with agents beyond chat using visual and interactive canvases.
- Move chats: Continue a chat in another folder or a new Git worktree without losing conversation history.
- Markdown editor: Work on Markdown files more efficiently with features like pasting images, renaming file links, or breadcrumb navigation.
- Enterprise management: Enforce agent sandboxing and permission policies while controlling which permission modes developers can use.
- Redesigned model picker: Quickly switch between Copilot and BYOK contributed models, and manage effort levels and context windows more intuitively.

items.title: Copilot harness
items.text:
The Copilot harness is powered by the Copilot SDK, a shared foundation that helps align behavior, capabilities, and improvements across Copilot products. In VS Code, the Copilot harness runs sessions through the Agent Host, which lets sessions continue in the background and be accessed from both the VS Code editor window and the Agents window.

The Copilot harness has been available from the harness picker in the chat input. Based on overwhelmingly positive and valuable feedback, we're progressively rolling it out as the default harness for new sessions in VS Code. When you start a new session, Copilot in the harness picker indicates that the session will use the Copilot harness.

Thank you to everyone who has shared feedback. We're actively using it to shape the experience. One example is reintroducing Ask as a built-in agent in the Copilot harness. Your feedback showed that a dedicated read-only experience remains valuable. Select Ask from the agent picker to use it.

items.title: Canvases (Preview)
items.text:
Setting: chat.canvases.enabled

Canvases are interactive interfaces to collaborate with an agent. A canvas opens beside the chat, where you and the agent can inspect and update the same artifact instead of coordinating solely through prompts.

For example, use a Kanban canvas to plan and track implementation work. You can create and move cards directly, while the agent can break a feature into tasks, update their status, or add newly discovered work. Canvases work in both the VS Code editor window and the Agents window, and canvas extensions are also supported in the GitHub Copilot app.

Canvases are available in Preview in the VS Code desktop app for local sessions that use the Copilot harness. Enable chat.canvases.enabled, and then start a new session with the Copilot harness.

Every canvas is provided by a canvas extension.

items.title: Move chats between folders and worktrees
items.text:
Previously, if you started investigating a task in one folder and then wanted to implement it in a Git worktree, or continue in a different repository, you had to start a new chat and rebuild the context.

In the Agents window, you can now ask the agent to move the current chat to another folder or into a new Git worktree, and it keeps the conversation history intact. Changing the workspace also works for chats that already have a workspace, and the agent can isolate work in a new worktree.

Ask the agent with a natural-language prompt, for example:

``prompt
Continue this task in a new Git worktree of the current repository before implementing it.
``

The agent finishes the current turn, moves the chat, and shows a notice when the workspace changes. Then it continues the task automatically in the new location. Edits and commands run in the new location while your original checkout stays unchanged.

items.title: Session-scoped layout in the Agents window (Experimental)
items.text:
Setting: sessions.experimental.layoutScope (Agents window only)

Previously, when you switched between sessions in the Agents window, VS Code shared layout settings such as editor visibility, details, and panel visibility across sessions. If you're used to VS Code remembering the layout for each workspace, sharing the layout across sessions can be disruptive.

With the new experimental sessions.experimental.layoutScope setting, you can choose how much of the layout each session remembers. Reload the window after you change the setting. It supports the following values:
- session-shared (default): The current behavior. A session and its nested sessions share the same editors and selected panel views. Editor, details, and bottom panel visibility are shared across existing workspace sessions.

items.title: Customize the Agents window panel layout
items.text:
You can now choose how the bottom panel is aligned in the Agents window. Right-click a panel tab, select Align Panel, and choose one of the following layouts:
- Center aligns the panel beneath the chat area, leaving more room for the side pane.
- Justify extends the panel across the full width of the window.

Your selection is saved per profile and preserved when maximizing or restoring the panel.

items.title: Quickly identify the active harness
items.text: Chat titles show the active harness name, such as Copilot or Codex, so you can identify it without opening the harness picker or hovering over the session list.

items.title: Stop background shells
items.text:
In Copilot harness sessions, the background shells pill above the chat input lists the commands that the agent is still running in the background. When one of those commands is no longer useful, for example a test run that you want to restart or a command that runs longer than expected, you can stop it instead of waiting for it to finish.

Select the Background Shells pill, select a shell to open its details, and then select Stop Shell next to its command. Only that command ends, and the shell leaves the list. You can reach Stop Shell with the keyboard, and screen readers announce when the shell stops.

Stopping a shell is only available for attached shells, which the agent runs as part of its current request. Detached shells run independently of the agent and can't be stopped from this interface.

Shell details also show each shell's full description above its command, even when the list truncates it.

items.title: Stateful responses for BYOK custom endpoints
items.text:
If your bring-your-own-key (BYOK) model uses a stateless Responses API, set "statefulResponses": false on its model entry in chatLanguageModels.json to send full conversation history with each request.

See Custom Endpoint configuration for details.

items.title: Windows sandboxing for Local harness is no longer supported
items.text: Windows sandboxing for terminal commands in Local agent sessions has been deprecated. For sandboxed command execution on Windows, use an Agent Host session. See the Agent Host sandboxing documentation for details.

items.title: Redesigned model picker
items.text:
Copilot and bring-your-own-key (BYOK) providers offer many models, each with strengths for different tasks. The redesigned model picker makes it easier to choose and switch models as your work changes.

The model picker uses a tabbed interface to separate Copilot and BYOK models.

When you hover over a model in the list, you can further configure its thinking level and context window size.

items.title: Editing mode closer to the Markdown source
items.text: When you edit Markdown, each source line appears on a separate visual line, making the document structure easier to follow. Read-only mode continues to render Markdown as before.

items.title: Paste images
items.text: To add an image, for example a screenshot, to your Markdown document, simply paste it directly into the Markdown editor, like you could already do in the text editor. This makes it easier to include visual content without having to save and insert files manually.

items.title: Rename file links
items.text: The Markdown editor now supports Rename Symbol (kb(editor.action.rename)), so you can rename file links in place and have the changes reflected throughout your document.

items.title: Outline and breadcrumbs
items.text: The Markdown editor integrates with the Outline view and breadcrumbs, making it easier to inspect the heading structure and jump to a section.

items.title: Copy code blocks
items.text: Like the Markdown preview, code blocks in the Markdown editor display a copy button on hover. This makes it easy to copy multiline code fragments without accidentally editing the content.

items.title: Merging document highlights from different providers
items.text:
Setting: editor.occurrencesHighlightFromAllProviders

Enable editor.occurrencesHighlightFromAllProviders to merge document highlights from all providers. By default, VS Code uses highlights only from the highest-priority provider.

items.title: Python
items.text:
This release includes fixes for environment discovery, interpreter selection, and terminal activation in the Python Environments Extension.
- Environment discovery: Python installations managed by uv now appear under Global. Selecting an interpreter by path adds its virtual environment to the environment list, and deleting a virtual environment outside VS Code updates the selection.
- Project-specific environments: Automatic selection now prefers a project's own virtual environment over nested environments. Conda environment selection and Poetry package operations respect project scope, and background refreshes no longer overwrite newer interpreter selections.
- Interpreter configuration: Fixed resolution of ${workspaceFolder}, relative paths, and commands such as python3 in python.defaultInterpreterPath. The project-view environment selector now includes Enter Interpreter Path.

items.title: Automatically move policy-managed chats to Copilot Agent Host
items.text:
Enterprise managed settings let administrators govern agent permissions and sandboxing. When your organization configures a nonempty permissions object or sets sandbox.enabled to true, VS Code now requires the Copilot harness in Agent Host for full chat sessions, to be able to enforce these policies.

Opening an existing, unarchived Local chat automatically moves it to Copilot, preserving the transcript and unsent draft, including attachments. Nothing is sent automatically. The new chat uses its normal model and permission defaults under current organization policy.

VS Code archives the original chat only after the new chat opens successfully. If you switch away while the move is in progress, the original stays unchanged and the unopened destination is removed.

While these policies apply, Claude, Codex, and terminal chat are unavailable. Editor inline chat remains available for limited read and edit tasks.

items.title: Temporarily keep the Local harness
Manage Copilot permission modes independently
Windows numeric policies support DWORD values
items.text: On Windows, policies that accept numeric values support DWORDs and QWORDs.

items.title: New deprecations in this release
items.text: - Windows sandboxing for Local harness is no longer supported

items.title: Release highlights
items.text:
This release makes the Copilot harness the default for new sessions and adds tools to compare models, reclaim storage, run models locally, and navigate file changes.
- Copilot harness by default: The default for new sessions, built on the Copilot SDK, lets you switch between editor and Agents window.
- Compare models (Preview): Run the same task with multiple models in the Agents window, then compare and combine their solutions.
- Reclaim worktree storage (Experimental): Free disk space by reviewing and removing inactive agent session worktrees.
- On-device models (Experimental): Run MAI Code 1.1 Flash locally on your device for your agent tasks.
- Multi-diff file list (Experimental): Keep an overview of and jump between changed files in the multi-file diff editor.

items.title: Copilot harness as the default
items.text:
The Copilot harness is now the default for new sessions in VS Code. It's our latest harness, built on the Copilot SDK, a shared foundation that helps align behavior, capabilities, and improvements across Copilot products.

When you start a new session, Copilot in the harness picker indicates that the session uses the Copilot harness:

In VS Code, you can keep Copilot harness sessions running in the background and access them from both the VS Code editor window and the Agents window. These sessions run through the Agent Host.

Thank you so much to everyone who has shared valuable feedback. This release includes more improvements shaped directly by your feedback.

We're continuing to improve performance and reduce latency based on the scenarios and setups you share. For example, reports of long waits before chat responses helped us reduce delays caused by MCP servers that don't finish loading their tools.

items.title: Discard changes from more changesets in the Agents window
items.text:
The Changes view in the Agents window lets you see all the modifications made by the agent. Until now, discarding pending changes was only available in the Uncommitted Changes changeset.

In this release, the Branch Changes, Session Changes, and Last Turn Changes changesets also offer the possibility to discard changes. Select Discard Changes on a file in the Changes view or in the multi-file diff editor. What VS Code discards depends on the changeset:
- Branch Changes: restores the file to its version where the branch diverged from its base branch, and deletes files that the branch added.
- Session Changes: reverts the session's edits to the file and keeps changes made outside the session, such as your own edits.
- Last Turn Changes: reverts only the latest turn's edits to the file and keeps all other changes to it.

items.title: Compare model results (Preview)
items.text:
Setting: sessions.chat.compareAgents.enabled (Agents window only)

Compare how different models and harnesses approach the same coding task. Run attempts in parallel, review their results, and combine ideas into one solution.

To get started, enable sessions.chat.compareAgents.enabled in the Agents window, then select Compare Models in the model picker.
- Choose the approaches to compare: Select two or more models to attempt your task independently. You can mix Copilot, Claude, and Codex harnesses and configure different reasoning levels.
- Run the attempts: Enter one prompt and start all selected attempts together.
- Follow progress side by side: Each attempt runs in its own session, so you can compare its approach and open the worktree or changes at any time.
- Evaluate and combine the results: Optionally select a Judge model to evaluate the attempts and recommend a solution.

items.title: Tab shortcuts in an empty side pane
items.text:
When you closed every tab in the Agents window side pane, the editor area was left blank, and you had to find the Add Tab (+) menu to get back to your session's changes or files.

The empty editor area now lists the tabs you can add, such as Changes, Files, Browser, and Search, each with its icon and keyboard shortcut. Select an entry to open that tab. If you have a canvas extension installed, a Canvas entry lists the available canvases. When you switch to a session whose editor area is empty, VS Code shows this list instead of reopening the Changes and Files tabs automatically.

items.title: Session Activity Bar (Experimental)
items.text:
Sessions: sessions.showSessionActivityBar, sessions.sessionActivityBar.showLayoutActions

The Session Activity Bar brings a session's Changes, Files, Browser, and available canvases next to the side pane, keeping these editors and artifacts visually connected to where they open. You can still open session artifacts from the pills at the top of the session.

The Session Activity Bar is a slim vertical strip of icons at the right edge of the active chat. Select an icon to open that tab in the side pane. If the side pane is closed, it opens with that tab active. If the tab is already open, VS Code focuses it instead of opening a second copy. If you have a canvas extension installed, a Canvas entry opens a submenu of the available canvases.

You can drag the Session Activity Bar up or down by its grip to move it out of your way, and double-click the grip to reset its position. When you split the chat area, only the focused group shows the Activity Bar.

items.title: Find and create files from the empty Files tab (Experimental)
items.text:
Setting: sessions.experimental.emptyFileEditorActions

In the Agents window, the Files tab was blank when no file was open, so you had to switch to the Files view to find or create a file in your session's folder.

When you enable sessions.experimental.emptyFileEditorActions, the empty Files tab shows a search box and a New File action. The search works like Quick Open (kb(workbench.action.quickOpen)), with the same ranking, highlights, and file icons, and it only finds files in the folders of the current session. Select a result to open it in the editor, or select New File to create a file in the session's folder. When you close the file, the search box returns.

items.title: Improved performance when opening large chats
items.text:
Opening a long Agent Host chat in the Agents window used to freeze the window for up to half a minute while the chat's history was restored. In this release, history is restored in small slices instead of one long blocking task, so the window stays responsive. Opening, switching back to, and reloading large chats is significantly faster.

| Scenario | Chat | Time to open: 1.142 → 1.143 | Window unresponsive: 1.142 → 1.143 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cold open | Chat A (~1,150 requests, ~530 MB history) | 35.6 s → 9.0 s | 28.3 s → 0.6 s |
| Cold open | Chat B (~1,450 requests, ~200 MB history) | 20.3 s → 3.0 s | 20.3 s → 0.4 s |
| Re-open | Chat A | 26.7 s → 0.6 s | 26.8 s → 0.3 s |
| Re-open | Chat B | 16.4 s → 0.4 s | 16.4 s → 0.2 s |
| Reload window | Chat A | 26.7 s → 2.9 s | 25.3 s → 0.9 s |
| Reload window | Chat B | 22.3 s → 2.2 s | 20.8 s → 0.4 s |

_Median of three runs on macOS, with real chats from day-to-day development.

items.title: Reclaim storage from inactive worktrees (Experimental)
items.text:
Setting: chat.agentSessions.sessionStorageCleanupSuggestion.enabled (Agents window only)

Worktrees are very useful for letting agents work on multiple features simultaneously without interfering with each other's changes. Over time, inactive worktrees can accumulate and consume significant disk space.

Run Chat: Open Worktree Cleanup from the Command Palette to see how much disk space inactive agent session worktrees use and remove the ones you no longer need. Filter sessions by how long they have been inactive, review each worktree's size, and select the worktrees to clean up.

Cleaning up marks the selected sessions as done and deletes their worktrees. You can restore a session later to recreate its worktree. Active, running, needs-input, and pinned sessions are protected from cleanup.

The cleanup editor lets you configure automatic cleanup for sessions with merged pull requests and control whether VS Code suggests cleanup when session storage grows large.

items.title: Run Copilot models on your device (Experimental)
items.text:
Laptops such as the new Surface Laptop Ultra, powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark with up to 128 GB of unified memory, have enough GPU memory to run a capable coding model locally. On-device models let you use that hardware with Copilot: download MAI Code 1.1 Flash from the new On This Device tab in the model picker and chat with it in Copilot harness sessions, with model processing on your device.

VS Code downloads and manages the model for you. Responses that run on your device are labeled On-device and don't use AI credits. To let Auto route suitable requests to the on-device model with cloud fallback, turn on Use in Auto on the model's details page.

To get started:
- Install a llama.cpp build that supports the model
- Set chat.copilot.localModel.llamaServerPath to its llama-server executable
- Enable chat.copilot.localModel.enabled

On-device models require GitHub sign-in and an NVIDIA GPU with 96 GB or more of GPU memory.

Learn more about on-device models.

items.title: Bring your own OpenAI model to Voice Mode (Preview)
items.text:
Settings: agents.voice.enabled, agents.voice.useBYOKVoiceModel

Use your own OpenAI API key and live model for voice-driven coding conversations instead of the hosted Voice Mode backend. Add your OpenAI key in the Language Models editor, enable agents.voice.enabled, and set agents.voice.useBYOKVoiceModel to a live model ID, like gpt-live-1 that your key can access.

items.title: Manage sandbox certificate trust
items.text:
Sandbox certificate trust management is available for agent hosts running Windows or macOS.

The sandbox credential proxy lets tools authenticate to approved services without exposing real authentication tokens to sandboxed processes. It gives tools placeholder credentials, then substitutes the real credentials when forwarding requests to approved destinations. For HTTPS requests, this requires the proxy to present its own TLS certificates, which the tools must trust.

Copilot supplies a certificate bundle for tools that support it. Some tools instead rely on the operating system's certificate trust store and can encounter certificate errors when the proxy's certificate authority (CA) isn't trusted. Installing the CA improves compatibility with these tools. Domain filtering alone does not require CA installation: the built-in local proxy can check destinations and tunnel HTTPS traffic without decrypting it.

items.title: Change session sandboxing when policy permits
items.text:
If your organization's managed policy permits sandbox bypass, you can turn sandboxing off for an individual Copilot harness session without changing your global settings. Use the Sandboxing for terminal toggle in the session permissions menu in either the editor or the Agents window. Administrators can continue to require sandboxing by disallowing bypass, which keeps the toggle on and locked.

Changes remain subject to approval by the agent runtime. If a change is rejected, VS Code shows an error and restores the last applied sandbox state. The collapsed permissions control and the reopened menu reflect that state.

items.title: Open canvases from the chat menu (Preview)
items.text:
Setting: chat.canvases.enabled

VS Code 1.142 introduced canvases (Preview), which are shared, interactive surfaces for collaborating with agents.

In this release, you can now open available canvases from New Chat (+) > Canvas in the editor window, without asking Copilot to open them.

When canvas support is enabled and you have canvas extensions installed, the submenu appears _after your first message_ in a Copilot harness session. You can also open canvases from the + menu in the Agents window.

Learn about installing, creating, and using canvases with the Copilot harness.

items.title: See output from detached background shells
items.text:
In Copilot harness sessions, the agent can start commands that need to continue running after it responds in a detached background shell. A dev server or a file watcher are common examples of such commands.

Previously, you couldn't view the output of detached background shells, for example to check whether a dev server started successfully. Detached shells now stream their output like attached shells. Select the Background Shells pill, and then select a detached shell to watch its output as the command runs. The shell's terminal output in the chat response also keeps updating after the agent finishes its response. When the command exits, the shell leaves the list, and the chat response keeps the command's output and exit status.

You can now also stop detached shells, which was previously only available for attached shells. When you no longer need a dev server or watcher, select Stop Shell in the shell's details.

items.title: Diagnostic highlight limits
items.text:
To improve diagnostic visibility in files with many reported problems, the editor highlight limit has increased from 500 to 5,000 diagnostics per file.

A warning in the editor's language status indicator indicates when diagnostics or their highlights are limited for performance reasons:
- Diagnostic source limit: Each extension diagnostic collection can provide up to 1,000 diagnostics per file. If a collection exceeds this limit, the warning indicates that some diagnostics are not shown.
- Editor highlight limit: The editor highlights up to 5,000 diagnostics per file across all sources. If this limit is exceeded, the warning indicates that only 5,000 diagnostics are highlighted.

If both limits are reached, the warning reports both conditions. Hover over the language status indicator in the Status Bar to view the details.

items.title: Multi-file diff editor file list (Experimental)
items.text:
Setting: multiDiffEditor.experimental.fileList

Navigate changes from commits, stashes, and agent sessions with a file list beside the multi-file diff view. Enable multiDiffEditor.experimental.fileList to try it.

Each file in the list has a status letter: A (added), M (modified), D (deleted), or R (renamed). As you scroll, the list highlights the file you're viewing. Select a file in the list to jump to its diff. Open Files View & Position in the editor toolbar's More Actions (...) menu to choose View as List or View as Tree, and to place the files On the Left or On the Right of the diffs.

items.title: Dynamic headers for managed OpenTelemetry
Managed model defaults
items.text:
New Copilot harness chats use your organization's managed defaults, even when you configure chat.defaultModel to another preference. The model picker and setting now explain which defaults apply. You can still change models and supported options per chat.

For example, the following configuration defaults new chats to Auto with the Intelligence tier in enterprise-managed settings:

``json
{
"model": "auto",
"autoTier": "intelligence"
}
``

items.title: Why Local is disabled
items.text:
When enterprise policy requires the Copilot harness, the Local harness now stays visible but is disabled in the harness picker, with a Learn why link explaining the restriction.

Copilot is required to enforce nonempty managed permissions.deny rules or sandbox.enabled: true, unless the temporary override below applies. Other permissions.* settings and an empty deny list do not trigger this requirement.

Administrators can prohibit Local with these enterprise-managed settings, not user settings:

``json
{
"vscode": {
"temporaryAllowLocalHarness": false,
"temporaryDefaultToLocalHarness": false
}
}
`

| Setting | Description |
| --- | --- |
| vscode.temporaryAllowLocalHarness | false prohibits Local, Claude, and Codex harnesses, overriding the temporary default below. true does not override other policies. |
| vscode.temporaryDefaultToLocalHarness | true` keeps Local available and suppresses automatic Copilot routing, including deny-list and sandbox requirements.

items.title: Fewer interruptions while organization settings load
items.text: Copilot harness sessions and model changes now wait for slow organization settings to load, with progress and a retry option on failure. You can still select Stop while you're waiting. Organization restrictions apply before requests run.

items.title: Fewer approval prompts for managed tools
items.text: Assisted permissions no longer prompt again for eligible managed tool requests they approve. One-time limits, managed denials, and sandbox restrictions still apply.

items.title: Managed plugins install automatically
Claude and Codex sessions
items.text: When policy requires the Copilot harness, existing Claude and Codex sessions remain visible in the sessions list, so you still can continue them with the Copilot harness. Creating new Claude or Codex sessions remains disabled in this scenario.

items.title: Install GitHub Copilot CLI with VS Code
items.text:
We now make it easier for you to get started with the GitHub Copilot CLI by letting you install it with the VS Code installer.

Note: Organizations can choose to disable this option via the Managed AI Settings.
- Windows

The VS Code installer on Windows now includes an option to install GitHub Copilot CLI. If you already have it installed, this option is not presented. Find more details in Set up the copilot command on Windows.
- Linux

The VS Code Linux installers add a copilot executable into the user path.

If you run the copilot command in the terminal, it will either prompt you to install GitHub Copilot CLI if it's not installed, or run GitHub Copilot CLI if it is already installed.
- macOS

On macOS, you are prompted to install GitHub Copilot CLI when you add VS Code to the $PATH environment variable via the Command Palette in VS Code.

items.title: Release recap
items.text:
The road to GitHub Universe (join us virtually!) is paved with lots of pull requests! So, let's take a step back and look at what we've shipped recently.
- Remember when agent sessions would stop as soon as you closed your client? We built the Agent Host, a separate process that keeps your agents running, on your local machine or remotely.
- With language servers in mind, we designed the Agent Host Protocol (AHP) to allow any client to interact with agent sessions. All of sudden, session continuity across VS Code, Copilot CLI, GitHub Copilot App, and github.com lets you pick up right where you left off.
- The Agents window lets you manage your agents across workspaces and environments from a single interface, whether you kick off things yourself or use automations to handle repetitive tasks.
- By default, agents are now powered by the Copilot harness, the same harness used in Copilot Code Review, the Copilot CLI, the Copilot App, and Copilot Cloud sessions.

items.title: Release highlights
items.text:
This release helps you keep agent work moving across environments, find the right models for each task, and stay in control of changes and tool calls.
- Session continuity: Manage remotes in one place and keep sessions and automations running even when your computer is off.
- Copilot Fusion and model comparisons: Let Copilot choose and orchestrate models, or compare models side by side.
- Image generation (Preview): Create and edit images directly in chat.
- Computer use (Experimental): Let agents use desktop apps on your computer.
- Working set (Experimental): Keep or undo agent file edits in the editor.
- Assisted permissions: Reduce interruptions with automatic approval for tool calls that pass a risk check.
- Customization marketplace and Copilot connectors (Preview): Discover skills and plugins for your workflow, and bring context from Slack, Notion, and other services into your agent sessions.

items.title: Run and continue Copilot tasks in the cloud
items.text:
Cloud sessions let you run Copilot tasks from VS Code without keeping your development machine online. Your repository and tools run in a managed environment on GitHub's infrastructure.

From the Chat view in the editor window or the Agents window, you can:
- Select Cloud and choose a GitHub repository to start a task.
- Send follow-up instructions, respond to approval requests, and review the agent's changes.
- Reopen an existing cloud session from the sessions list to continue the same conversation.

Your cloud sessions are also accessible from other Copilot clients. For example, you can check progress on GitHub.com or in the GitHub Mobile app, then return to VS Code to continue working.

Cloud sessions use a separate workspace. Local uncommitted changes aren't automatically copied. The new cloud experience requires a paid Copilot plan and is subject to organization policies.

items.title: Manage remote environments
items.text:
VS Code lets you run agents and perform development tasks across different (remote) environments. To make it easier to manage these environments, we're introducing the Remote Environments dialog, which brings your GitHub Environments, Dev Tunnels, WSL distributions, and SSH hosts together in one place.

Select Manage Remote Environments at the bottom of the Environment picker to see the status of each remote, connect or disconnect, and choose which remotes should be visible in the pickers.

Learn more about remote agent sessions.

items.title: Cloud Automations (Preview)
items.text:
Setting: chat.automations.cloud.enabled

Create and manage Copilot cloud automations directly in the Agents window. Enabled by default, they run on GitHub infrastructure on a schedule or in response to repository events, even when your computer is off.

To create a cloud automation, you can ask an agent to set one up for you, or use the Create Automation button in the Automations view in the Agents window.

With cloud automations, you can:
- Set up automations that run in response to issue or pull request events: Act automatically when activity happens in your repository. For example, automatically triaging issues as they get assigned to you.
- Build shared workflows in the cloud with your team: Create automations that are visible to everyone with access to the repository and act as Copilot.
- Control exactly when your agent runs and what it can do: Limit allowed tools and add filters for precise control over your automations.

items.title: Agent Host Protocol v1.0
items.text:
We've published the first version of the Agent Host Protocol, the protocol that VS Code uses to communicate with its agents locally and on remote machines, including for cloud automations. It's an open, extensible protocol designed to be an easy way to build custom UI's for your agents, or build agent platforms that plug into any UI that speaks it.

You can add a websocket-based agent host to your VS Code instance via the command Agents: Add Remote Agent Host... in the Agents window, and run code agent endpoints to get the endpoints for your editor's running agent host. We publish libraries in six languages and have found agents are good at making clients and hosts using them.

You can read more about the protocol and find additional resources on the Agent Host Protocol website.

items.title: Route and orchestrate models with GitHub Copilot Fusion
items.text:
Instead of picking a model for each task, select Copilot Fusion in the model picker and let Copilot intelligently route requests and orchestrate models for you. Copilot Fusion brings together Project HydraFusion's multi-model orchestration and Copilot auto model selection's task-aware model selection to balance performance and cost efficiency.

For each request, Copilot Fusion chooses the models, reasoning effort, and execution pattern for your task. For example, one model completes a simple task, while for harder tasks one model drafts a solution and other models review or critique it. Hover over the effort level below a response to see which models were used.

Choose an effort level to balance quality and cost: Standard for everyday coding work, High for more demanding tasks, and Max for the most complex tasks.

You're billed for each model that Copilot Fusion uses at its standard rate. Through November 30, 2026, paid Copilot plans receive a 30% discount when using Copilot Fusion.

items.title: Compare models and harnesses by default and in more projects
items.text:
Setting: sessions.chat.compareAgents.enabled

Model comparisons run the same prompt across models for side-by-side review. They are enabled by default for eligible new sessions in the Agents window, unless overridden by user settings or experiments.

In this release, we expanded model comparison to more scenarios:
- Explore ideas without a project: Run independent attempts from a folderless Chat, without a Git repository, judge, or synthesizer.
- Start with a local or empty repository: A Git remote and an initial commit are no longer required. For repositories without commits, each isolated attempt starts from a snapshot of non-ignored working files without changing your source branch or index.

To open comparison setup from the keyboard, press kb(sessions.compareModels) from an eligible chat input or model picker.

items.title: Image generation in Copilot (Preview)
items.text:
Setting: chat.copilot.imageGeneration.model, chat.copilot.imageGeneration.watermark.

Agents can generate images from your prompts with GPT Image 2.5 Flare. Ask the agent to create an image for your website, a chat background, a new icon, or a website wireframe. You can also add an existing image as chat context and ask the agent to modify it or generate variations.

The default image model is GPT Image 2.5 Flare. To disable image generation, set chat.copilot.imageGeneration.model to off. Image generation requires access to the selected model and uses AI credits in addition to those used by the conversation model.

Additionally, set chat.copilot.imageGeneration.watermark to true to add a perceptible Made with AI watermark to your image.

items.title: Let agents use desktop apps with computer use
items.text:
Setting: chat.agentHost.computerUse.enabled

Some tasks happen in desktop apps rather than in your code or the terminal. With Computer Use, the agent can see and control apps on your computer. Computer Use works in Copilot harness sessions that run on your own macOS or Windows machine.

When a task needs Computer Use, the agent asks you to allow turning it on, or you can run /computer on. Computer Use stays on for Copilot until you run /computer off.

Learn more about Computer Use in the documentation.

items.title: Canvases (Preview)
items.text:
Setting: chat.canvases.enabled

Previously introduced in VS Code 1.142, Canvases are shared, interactive surfaces where you and the agent can inspect and update the same artifact. This release makes canvases easier to find, manage, and open.

#### Manage canvases in the Agent Customizations editor

The Agent Customizations editor's Canvases section lists the canvases available to the active Copilot session and groups their contributing canvas extensions by source. To see it, open a Copilot session with at least one message in it, and open the Agent Customizations editor from there.

Under the Browse section, select Canvases to find plugins whose metadata indicates that they provide canvases. Some canvas-capable plugins might not have that metadata and would appear under Plugins instead. Learn how to manage canvas extensions.

#### Open canvases from the Add Context menu

In chats in the editor or Agents window, select Add Context (+) > Canvas... to open or refocus an available canvas.

items.title: Assisted permissions are generally available
items.text:
Agents can make many tool calls to accomplish a task. Approving every tool call ensures that each action is explicitly authorized, but it can become cumbersome for frequent or low-risk calls. Giving the agent full autonomy might be risky and result in unintended actions or security issues.

With assisted permissions (now generally available for Copilot sessions), the agent performs an LLM-based risk assessment for each tool call and automatically approves low-risk calls. When a call is deemed higher risk or if the risk cannot be determined, the tool call still requires explicit user approval. This approach gives you a balance between convenience and security.

Select Assisted permissions in the permissions picker to have an LLM assess tool-call risk. Calls it approves run without prompting, while other calls still require your confirmation. Assisted permissions require Folder isolation and might be restricted by your organization.

items.title: Session composer controls (Experimental)
items.text:
Starting a new agent session is something you do often, so we've grouped the key settings at the top and added shortcuts for quick access.

#### Choose the environment first

With session continuity, where you run an agent session and where you access it from is completely up to you. So, when you create a new session in the Agents window, selecting the environment where the session runs is likely the first thing you do. Use the environment picker to choose from This Computer, Cloud, an eligible remote host, or a supported Dev Container.

The other configuration options will change based on the selected environment. For example, creating a session locally will let you specify the branch and worktree code isolation options.

To hide the Environment picker, disable sessions.chat.experimental.environmentPicker.

items.title: Copilot harness as the default
items.text:
The Copilot harness continues to be the default for new sessions in VS Code. It's our latest harness, built on the Copilot SDK, a shared foundation that helps align behavior, capabilities, and improvements across Copilot products.

When you start a new session, Copilot in the harness picker indicates that the session uses the Copilot harness:

In VS Code, you can keep Copilot harness sessions running in the background and access them from both the VS Code editor window and the Agents window. These sessions run through the Agent Host.

#### Review Copilot file edits with the working set (Experimental)

Setting: chat.editor.workingSet.enabled

The Copilot harness records edits made through agent tools in a working set, so you can review and decide which changes to keep or undo, just like in the Local harness. Use the inline Keep and Undo controls in the editor for individual changes, or manage files and all pending changes from the working set above the chat input.

items.title: Copilot Memory in the Copilot harness
items.text:
Copilot harness sessions can now use Copilot Memory, the same cloud memory service that other Copilot surfaces like Copilot CLI, Copilot cloud agent, and Copilot code review also use.

Agents recall relevant repository facts and your preferences when a session starts, and store new learnings as you work, so you don't have to repeat the same context in every new conversation.

Memories are stored as repository facts, which are shared with others who have access to the repository, or as user preferences, which apply across your repositories. Ask the agent to remember a convention or preference, and state the scope when it matters:

``prompt
Across all my repositories, remember that I prefer concise commit message subjects.
``

Copilot Memory is enabled by default and respects your Copilot Memory settings on GitHub and your organization's policies. You can review and delete your memories on GitHub at any time.

Learn more about using memory with agents.

items.title: Manage worktree storage (Experimental)
items.text:
Setting: chat.agentSessions.sessionStorageCleanupSuggestion.enabled

Last release, we introduced worktree storage cleanup for agent sessions to help you reclaim disk space used by worktrees. This release adds more ways to find the worktrees you want to remove:
- See all past worktrees: The Any time option is selected by default, to let you review recent worktrees as well as older ones.
- Find worktrees by workspace: Each row shows its workspace, and a workspace filter narrows the results. Changing the workspace filter clears the selection.

When cleanup suggestions are enabled and a local worktree's disk has less than 5 GB available, the Agents window provides a suggestion below the sessions list to run worktree cleanup, regardless of worktree age or count. The suggestion opens cleanup with Any time selected.

items.title: Enable extensions in agents window
items.text: Extensions can run and be enabled or disabled directly from the Agents window. This requires extensions.experimental.agentsWindowManagement to be set to true.

items.title: GitHub Environments
items.text:
There is a new option for sharing your local agents with your other devices. The radio tower button in the upper right corner of the agents window previously shared your local agents over dev tunnels, but now you have the option to share with GitHub Environments as well.

What's the difference? Your GitHub Environment can be accessed from all GitHub Copilot apps, so you can start a session on your computer and continue it on the GitHub iOS app, or the Copilot desktop app, or https://github.com/copilot, even the Copilot CLI. You can also access it in VS Code from another device, by selecting the GitHub Environments option in the Agents Window picker.

You can also register a GitHub Environment from the code CLI with a command like this: code agent host --github-environment.

items.title: Connect services with Copilot connectors (Preview)
items.text:
Bring the Slack discussion behind a change, project context from Notion, or API documentation from Microsoft Learn into your agent sessions. Copilot connectors are GitHub-managed MCP servers that connect your agent to these services without local server setup or MCP configuration.

Open Browse, choose Copilot Connectors in the source menu, and select Connect on a service. Authorize access in your browser. Connect once and reuse the connection across supported Copilot clients signed in with the same account.

Connectors are enabled by default on all Copilot plans and work only with the Copilot harness. For Business and Enterprise, an administrator must enable Editor preview features. Your organization's MCP restrictions apply, and some services require administrator approval.

items.title: Discover marketplace customizations (Preview)
items.text:
Add skills, tools, and entire workflows to your agent without building them from scratch. Browse, the new home page for Customizations, brings together GitHub Feed and plugins from marketplaces configured by you or your enterprise.

Explore Editor's picks, Plan, build, and ship, and Connect your work, or search and filter by source or type. Open Browse or run Chat: Open Customizations to start.

Link to Browse from a README or team guide, optionally with a search. For example, Browse filtered to MCP servers.

GitHub Feed requires a supported harness and isn't available in Local sessions. For Copilot Business and Enterprise, an administrator must enable Editor preview features.

items.title: Richer editing for GitHub Copilot custom agents
items.text:
When you customize agents for the GitHub Copilot harness, completions, hovers, and validation help you choose available models, tools, and skills and catch configuration errors before you run the agent.
- Models: The model attribute offers Copilot model IDs as a single value or an ordered list of preferences.
- Tools: The tools attribute offers Copilot tool aliases, such as read, edit, and execute, alongside qualified client and extension tools.
- Skills: The skills attribute offers available skills, with descriptions and source information in completions and hovers.
- Configuration validation: Copilot-specific attributes and nested structures, including hooks and agent-scoped MCP servers, have completions, hovers, and validation. Unknown models, tools, and skills are only flagged after discovery has finished, so valid values aren't marked as errors while inventories are still loading.

items.title: Harness-aware defaults for custom agent editing
items.text: When your .agent.md file has no target attribute, the editor now uses the active customization harness to provide matching completions, hovers, and diagnostics. Switching harnesses refreshes this guidance without reopening the file. An explicit target: vscode or target: github-copilot continues to override the default.

items.title: Share links to plugins and customizations
items.text:
You can share deep links in a README or team guide to help others add an agent plugin marketplace, install a specific plugin, or open a page in the customization dialog.

| Action | Example link |
|--------|--------------|
| Add a marketplace | vscode://chat-plugin/add-marketplace?ref=owner/repo |
| Add a marketplace and install a named plugin | vscode://chat-plugin/install?source=owner/repo&plugin=plugin-name |
| Open the Plugins page with a search filter | vscode://chat-customizations/open?page=plugins&search=github |

Replace owner/repo with the marketplace's GitHub repository and plugin-name with the plugin's name in that marketplace. VS Code asks for confirmation before adding a marketplace or installing a plugin. These actions use a Copilot harness session; if none is available, VS Code asks before creating one. Only proceed if you trust the source, because plugins can run code on your machine.

items.title: Manage Copilot customizations with slash commands
items.text:
You can manage plugins, MCP servers, and skills without leaving the Chat view in a Copilot harness session. Type /plugin, /mcp, or /skills followed by a space to see the available subcommands.
- Plugins: List, install, update, enable, disable, or uninstall agent plugins. Use /plugin marketplace to manage marketplaces, or /plugin install to choose a plugin to install.
- MCP servers: Use /mcp show, /mcp enable, or /mcp disable with a server name to inspect or manage your MCP servers.
- Skills: Use /skills info with a skill name to inspect an available agent skill.

Completions suggest supported subcommands and relevant plugin, marketplace, server, or skill names. Available commands depend on the Copilot runtime, and results appear directly in chat.

The following video shows browsing the vscode-team-kit marketplace and installing the Session timeline plugin with /plugin install.

items.title: Move chats between sessions (Preview)
items.text:
Setting: chat.agentHost.moveChats.enabled

The Agents window lets you organize related conversations into sessions. Rearrange those conversations as your work evolves without starting over or losing their history.
- Drag a nested chat into another session, or drop it between that session's nested chats to choose its position.
- Right-click a nested chat and select Promote to Session to give it its own session. You can also drag it onto empty space in the sessions list.
- Drag a single-chat session onto another session to nest it there.
- Reorder nested chats by dragging them, or use Move Up and Move Down from their context menu. With focus in the sessions list, use kb(sessionsViewPane.moveChatUp) and kb(sessionsViewPane.moveChatDown).

Moves preserve the chat's working folder, including an existing worktree or a temporary folder for a chat without a workspace. A shared worktree remains available while another session still uses it.

items.title: Choose a workspace for nested sessions
items.text:
Previously, nested sessions inherited the workspace of their parent session. Now, you can choose a separate workspace for each nested session. This lets you work across repositories while keeping related conversations together in one session. For example, a frontend chat and a backend chat can work in different folders without splitting the task across separate sessions.

Select New Nested Session in the Agents window to open a composer with a folder picker that defaults to the parent session's folder. Choose a recent folder, browse to another folder, or select No Workspace for a chat with its own temporary folder.

For a Git repository, choose New Worktree and a branch to isolate the nested chat's file changes. The nested chat uses its parent session's agent and host. Agents that do not support multiple working directories offer only the parent session's folder.

items.title: Nested sessions in quick chats
items.text:
Follow up on a quick chat without mixing separate questions into one conversation or losing track of related discussions. For example, explore two approaches in separate nested sessions under the same quick chat, without opening a project folder.

Quick chats in the Agents window support nested sessions: select + on a quick chat or use New Nested Session from its context menu.

Each nested session starts with No Workspace selected and gets its own temporary folder, separate from the parent quick chat. The quick chat stays in the Chats section, keeping its related conversations together.

items.title: Custom icons and colors for session groups
items.text: Make workspace groups, environment groups (including remote hosts), and custom groups easier to recognize with custom icons and theme-aware colors. In the Agents window, open a group's context menu and select Change Icon... or Change Color.... Your choices persist across reloads and host reconnections, and Reset to default restores the icon or color independently. _#343576_

items.title: Voice conversations with session context (Experimental)
items.text:
Voice Mode (agents.voice.enabled) lets you discuss tasks aloud while the coding agent works. Use an OpenAI live model with your own API key (agents.voice.useBYOKVoiceModel) to ask questions such as 'Where were we?' or 'Which session needs input?' without starting a coding request.

The enabled-by-default agents.voice.sessionAwareness shares a bounded briefing of tracked sessions and recent active-chat context with OpenAI BYOK Voice Mode. It includes session titles, response summaries, pending prompt details, the selected model, and attachment names, but not attachment contents.

Voice Mode's animation uses a single color for a more conversational feel: you can jump in and speak at any time.

GPT Live conversations also handle follow-ups and ongoing work more predictably:
- Ask questions while the agent works and hear the answers, with other updates queued and read aloud afterward.

items.title: Localized voice approvals and clearer connection status (Experimental)
items.text:
Approve or reject GPT Live tool requests in your selected voice language (agents.voice.language), with support for 25 languages and English as a fallback. Answer questions with displayed choice labels, numbers, or free text where allowed. Ambiguous approvals still require an explicit answer or chat controls.

The voice language setting does not translate agent-provided questions or choices. Commands such as 'skip' and 'other' remain English-only.

items.title: Issue Reporter
items.text:
Settings: issueReporter.wizard.enabled, issueReporter.wizard.openLocation, issueReporter.additionalRepositories

Issues with clear steps, screenshots, and logs are faster for us to reproduce and fix. The new issue reporter, which you turn on with issueReporter.wizard.enabled, makes it easier for you to create high quality issues. You can capture screenshots and screen recordings without leaving VS Code, from the capture bar or with kb(workbench.action.issueReporter.captureScreenshot) and kb(workbench.action.issueReporter.toggleRecording).

This release makes these changes to the new issue reporter:
- The form fits on a single page instead of three steps.
- Attach other files that help us debug your issue, such as log files or zip archives. You can also paste or drop images and videos into the form.
- The reporter opens in its own window. To open it in an editor tab instead, set issueReporter.wizard.openLocation to editor.

items.title: Dialogs from terminal commands open in front of VS Code on Windows
items.text:
Setting: terminal.integrated.windowsReparentConsoleWindow

On Windows, some command-line tools open dialogs that could appear behind VS Code when run from the terminal. For example, the Azure PowerShell Connect-AzAccount sign-in picker opened behind the VS Code window, so the command looked stuck until you moved or minimized VS Code.

VS Code now makes the window that shows each local terminal the owner of that terminal's hidden console window, as Windows Terminal does. Dialogs that tools attach to their console window now open in front of the VS Code window the terminal is in.

This requires terminal.integrated.windowsUseConptyDll, which is enabled by default. To turn off this behavior, set terminal.integrated.windowsReparentConsoleWindow to false.

items.title: Clearer permission restrictions
Organization-managed session defaults
Managed settings loading progress
items.text: When organization settings load slowly, progress appears inline in the waiting chat instead of stacking notification toasts. Background loading no longer interrupts you.

items.title: Release highlights
items.text:
This week, your remote agent sessions feel a bit more local. Preview apps and use canvases right in VS Code, fine-tune automation schedules with cron, and turn down the noise in chat. And when you need a break, Blobby is ready to play.
- Remote agents: Preview apps and use interactive canvases from remote agent sessions without leaving the Agents window.
- Automations: Run recurring agent tasks on custom schedules beyond the built-in presets with cron.
- Agent verbosity: Keep chats concise or see the full details of the agent's reasoning and tool calls, your choice.
- File exclusions: Exclude folders while keeping the files you need visible and searchable.
- Fun: Take a short break with a platform-jumping game starring Blobby, the VS Code pet.

items.title: Browse over remote agent host connections (Preview)
items.text:
Setting: workbench.browser.enableRemoteProxy

When an agent session runs on a remote agent host, the integrated browser in the Agents window now loads pages through that host, as it already does in remote workspaces. When the agent starts a dev server on the remote machine, you can open it right in the Agents window to preview the app, validate the agent's changes, and give it feedback, as you would in a local session.

Enable workbench.browser.enableRemoteProxy to try it out, and file any issues you encounter in the VS Code repository.

items.title: Remote canvases (Preview)
items.text:
Settings: workbench.browser.enableRemoteProxy, chat.canvases.enabled

Thanks to the remote agent host connections support, you can now also use canvases that are hosted on a remote agent host.

Enable chat.canvases.enabled and workbench.browser.enableRemoteProxy to try it out, and file any issues you encounter in the VS Code repository.

items.title: Mix and match agent harnesses in one session (Preview)
items.text:
Setting: chat.agentHost.multipleChatProviders.enabled

Nested sessions let you keep related conversations together within a single main chat session. Previously, every nested session inherited its parent session's harness. If you wanted a second opinion from another agent, you had to start a separate session and lose that grouping.

In this release, nested sessions can use different harnesses than their parent session. For example, ask Claude to review the plan that a Copilot chat wrote, or give Codex the same task, side by side in the same session. When you create a new nested session, use the harness picker to switch to a different harness.

Each chat has its own model, agent, and permission levels, based on its harness. Changing them in one chat doesn't affect the others. When you move a chat, it keeps its history and continues with its selected harness. When you fork a nested session, it continues with the same configuration.

items.title: Cron schedules and custom agents for local automations
items.text:
Instead of manually running agent tasks one by one, you can use automations to schedule and run them automatically, either on demand or on a set schedule.

This release gives you more flexibility for local automations and keeps the Automations view focused on active work:
- Use cron schedules: Select Cron to enter a five-field cron expression when the other schedule presets aren't precise enough. The dialog validates the expression and describes the resulting schedule. Cron schedules are not available for cloud automations.
- Use workspace custom agents: Choose a custom agent from the selected workspace when you create or edit a local automation.
- Focus on active automations: Disabled automations appear in a collapsed Disabled automations section, so they don't obscure run history and active automations.

Learn more about creating and managing agent automations.

items.title: Pin canvases to sidebar (Experimental)
items.text:
Setting: chat.canvases.enabled

To make it easier to access frequently used canvases, you can now pin a canvas to appear in the left sidebar. To pin a canvas, open it and select the Add to Sidebar button above the canvas. Pinned canvases remain accessible in the sidebar even when you navigate away from them.

items.title: Copilot harness
items.text:
The Copilot harness continues to be the default for new sessions in VS Code. It's our latest harness, built on the Copilot SDK, a shared foundation that helps align behavior, capabilities, and improvements across Copilot products.

When you start a new session, Copilot in the harness picker indicates that the session uses the Copilot harness. In VS Code, you can keep Copilot harness sessions running in the background and access them from both the VS Code editor window and the Agents window. These sessions run through the Agent Host.

To help you adopt the Copilot harness with your existing workflows, we've added a Local-to-Copilot harness transition guide. It covers customization compatibility, session continuity, and organization rollout and verification.

Thank you for the feedback that continues to shape these improvements. Please continue filing issues about your experience, especially if a workflow or integration prevents your organization from moving off the Local harness.

items.title: Working set improvements (Experimental)
items.text:
Setting: chat.editor.workingSet.enabled

Last release, we introduced the working set for Copilot harness sessions, letting you review pending agent edits. You can keep or undo changes, as you could do with the Local harness.

We are further improving the working set experience in Copilot harness sessions:
- Files in WSL, Dev Containers, and SSH workspaces open from the working set on the correct host.
- When several tool calls edit the same file in parallel, the working set tracks those edits and the editor's inline review controls remain available after editing finishes.

The working set functionality remains enabled by default in the editor window. Learn more about reviewing agent edits with the working set, including which edits it tracks.

items.title: Improved guidance when required sandboxing is unavailable
items.text:
Agent sandboxing limits what terminal commands can access, like the file system and network resources. Your organization can require it with managed settings that disallow bypassing the sandbox.

If your organization requires sandboxing but your machine can't run it, the warning banner explains why terminal commands are blocked and how to resolve the problem. It shows the specific cause, such as a missing dependency, and links to troubleshooting steps.

If your account and organization support cloud sessions (Experimental), consider running agent tools in the cloud instead of on your machine.

items.title: Choose agent verbosity (Experimental)
items.text:
Setting: chat.persistentProgressVerbosity

Keep long chats readable, or follow the agent's reasoning and tool calls in detail when you need to understand its actions. Open the Chat view's More Actions menu and select View Mode:
- Conversation: Focus on the conversation. Reasoning and tool calls are grouped into collapsed sections between blocks of response text. Expand a section to inspect its details.
- Verbose: Follow each step with tool calls expanded, without an internal scrolling limit on tool groups.
- Compact (default): Preview tool calls while they run, then collapse completed groups to expandable summary rows.

You can switch modes without starting a new chat. The modes change how the conversation is displayed, not its context or the work the agent performs.

With persistent progress enabled, the active progress indicator stays above the chat input while you scroll back through a response. If you prefer an animated input border instead, enable chat.progressBorder.enabled.

items.title: Chat performance improvements
items.text:
Reopen and browse long Copilot harness chats more smoothly. VS Code reuses existing reasoning titles and renders terminal output as you reveal it. Terminal output in restored tool calls is rendered when you expand or reveal it, rather than all at once.

This release also reduces repeated progress updates and layout measurements when restoring and navigating long conversations.

items.title: Inline chat attachments (Experimental)
items.text:
Setting: chat.inlineAttachments.enabled

Keep file references and other context next to the instructions they belong to. Enable this setting to insert attachment pills at the cursor in your prompt, rather than in a separate row above the input.

Move across, select, or delete an attachment pill as a single character. Previous messages keep the pills inline, so references stay with the surrounding instructions.

Inline attachments are on by default in Insiders and off by default in Stable.

items.title: Attach files from anywhere on your computer
items.text:
Previously, to give chat a file outside your workspace, such as a screenshot or mockup on your desktop, you had to drag it in from your file manager or ask the agent to find it. Select Add Context (+) > Files to choose one or more files with the standard file dialog, even in a new chat without a workspace. In cloud sessions, the chooser lists only images.

When sandboxing is enabled in Copilot harness sessions, the agent can read the files and folders you attach, even when they're outside the workspace. Each attached path is readable for the rest of the session, but the agent can't write to it, and the access isn't saved to your settings. With Manual permissions, the agent no longer asks before reading an attached file. If your organization's managed settings define their own list of readable paths, attachments aren't added to it.

items.title: Support for tools provided by MCP apps
items.text:
MCP apps are interactive interfaces provided by MCP servers. They can now register tools that the language model can call in its next request.
